cards.front: What is an internal threat?
cards.back: A security threat from someone inside the organisation with legitimate access — e.g. employee sabotage (deliberate or accidental), theft/loss of equipment, data or software, or use of unauthorised software. Harder to detect than external threats.

cards.front: What human factors cause accidental data loss?
cards.back: Negligence, poor training, and not following security procedures — made worse by inadequate monitoring and a weak security culture.

cards.front: Name the named virus types in the spec.
cards.back: Boot sector, web script, macro, worm, rootkit, trojan, browser hijack and polymorphic. A virus attaches to a host file and replicates when run.

cards.front: What is a polymorphic virus?
cards.back: A virus that changes (mutates) its own code each time it spreads, so signature-based antivirus struggles to detect it.

cards.front: What is spyware? Give an example.
cards.back: Software that secretly gathers information and sends it to a third party. Examples: keylogger (records keystrokes to steal passwords), system monitor, stalkerware, tracking cookies.

cards.front: What is ransomware and its main defence?
cards.back: Malware that blocks access to data (usually by encrypting files) and demands payment. Types: encryptors, lockers, scareware, leakware. Best defence: tested OFFLINE backups so you can restore without paying.

cards.front: What is a bot / botnet?
cards.back: A bot is an infected device under remote attacker control. Many bots together form a botnet, used to send spam or launch DDoS attacks.

cards.front: Difference between DoS and DDoS?
cards.back: DoS = a single machine floods a target with traffic to make it unavailable. DDoS = many machines (a botnet) flood the target at once, making it harder to stop.

cards.front: Name the social engineering variants.
cards.back: Phishing (email), vishing (voice/phone), smishing (SMS), whaling (targets senior execs), spear phishing (targets a specific person), pretexting/impersonation, DNS spoofing.

cards.front: What is tailgating?
cards.back: Following an authorised person through a secure/controlled door to gain entry without using your own credentials. A physical social-engineering threat.

cards.front: Name the four types of impact of a cyber attack.
cards.back: Operational loss (can't function), financial loss (fines, compensation, lost profits), reputational loss (lost trust/reviews), and intellectual property loss (designs, trade secrets).

cards.front: What is the NCSC?
cards.back: The National Cyber Security Centre — the UK's cyber security authority. Publishes the latest threat reports, malware analysis and advisories, because threats change over time.

cards.front: What is the OWASP Top 10?
cards.back: A regularly updated list of the most critical web application security risks, produced by the Open Web Application Security Project. Used as a checklist during penetration testing.

cards.front: Name the three firewall port categories.
cards.back: Well-known/assigned (e.g. port 80 for HTTP), registered (used by OS and specific software), and dynamic/private (temporary/custom services). Open ports are a vulnerability.

cards.front: What is a zero-day exploit?
cards.back: A brand-new vulnerability that has no patch/fix yet, giving attackers a 'window of exploitation' before the developer can release a patch.

cards.front: What checks make a software download safe?
cards.back: Trusted source, HTTPS/lock symbol, a pre-install malware scan, and a hash check. Illegal copies may contain backdoors/malware and get no updates.

cards.front: Give three IoT security risks.
cards.back: Weak/no encryption, default passwords, lack of patches/updates, deployment by non-IT staff, insecure interfaces, and eavesdropping (always-listening devices).

cards.front: Name vulnerability assessment tools.
cards.back: Port scanner, network mapper/system discovery, registry checker, website vulnerability scanner, and vulnerability detection/management software.

cards.front: What is penetration testing?
cards.back: Authorised simulated attacks on a system to find weak spots, checked against known vulnerabilities (e.g. the OWASP Top 10), producing a report of findings.

cards.front: Name the three passive risk management measures.
cards.back: Risk transfer (pass it to a third party, e.g. insurance), risk avoidance (stop the activity), and risk acceptance (acknowledge and tolerate the risk).

cards.front: GDPR vs Computer Misuse Act — what does each cover?
cards.back: GDPR = protection of personal data and privacy rights. Computer Misuse Act 1990 = unauthorised access to, and modification of, computers and data (makes hacking illegal).

cards.front: List key GDPR principles.
cards.back: Lawfulness/fairness/transparency, limited to a stated purpose, accuracy, keep minimum data, store for minimum time, maintain confidentiality and integrity.

cards.front: Name GDPR personal rights.
cards.back: Right to access own data, be informed, have data corrected/removed/restricted, object to processing, data portability, and not be subject to a solely automated decision.

cards.front: Give examples of physical security measures.
cards.back: Site locks, card entry (NFC/RFID/QR/magnetic stripe), biometrics (fingerprint/iris/facial/voice), CCTV, security staff, alarms, protected cabling, staff training.

cards.front: Name the three backup types.
cards.back: Full (everything), Incremental (only changes since the LAST backup), Differential (all changes since the last FULL backup). Note: RAID and archiving are NOT backups.

cards.front: Signature scanning vs heuristics in antivirus?
cards.back: Signature scanning matches files against a database of KNOWN malware. Heuristics flag suspicious behaviour/content, catching NEW or unknown threats.

cards.front: Name the multi-factor authentication factor types.
cards.back: Knowledge (something you know, e.g. password), possession (something you have, e.g. USB key), inherence (something you are, e.g. fingerprint), plus location and behaviour factors.

cards.front: How does a USB security key work (MFA)?
cards.back: The USB key/chip contains a code/protocol that the server/system reads and checks to verify the user's identity — a 'possession' factor in multi-factor authentication.

cards.front: Compare DAC, Role-Based and Rule-Based access control.
cards.back: DAC: users control access to their own files. Role-Based (RBAC): access set by job role in the organisation. Rule-Based: admin sets rules for individual users.

cards.front: Benefit and drawback of trusted computing?
cards.back: Benefit: increased security / an extra layer of protection against attacks. Drawback: loss of user control, privacy and anonymity.

cards.front: Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption?
cards.back: Symmetric uses ONE shared secret key (e.g. AES) — fast but the key must be shared securely. Asymmetric uses a PUBLIC + PRIVATE key pair (e.g. RSA) — slower but no shared secret.

cards.front: Why is MAC address filtering only 'medium' security?
cards.back: It allows only listed device MAC addresses onto the Wi-Fi, but MAC addresses can be SPOOFED (faked) by an attacker, so it shouldn't be the only protection.

cards.front: What is an Evil Twin attack?
cards.back: An attacker sets up a fake wireless access point that imitates a legitimate one, tricking users into connecting so their traffic can be intercepted.

cards.front: Name principles of secure system design.
cards.back: Expect attacks and plan for them, run on fewest privileges (least privilege), assume the design is known (don't rely on secrecy), and comply with standards like ISO 27000.

cards.front: LAN vs WAN vs PAN?
cards.back: LAN = Local Area Network (one site). WAN = Wide Area Network (large geographic area, e.g. the internet). PAN = Personal Area Network (very short range, e.g. Bluetooth).

cards.front: Intranet vs extranet?
cards.back: Intranet = a private network for an organisation's own staff. Extranet = extends controlled access to selected outsiders such as suppliers or partners.

cards.front: Client/server vs peer-to-peer?
cards.back: Client/server has a central server controlling resources and security (easier to manage/secure). Peer-to-peer shares resources directly between devices with no central server.

cards.front: How does virtualisation improve security?
cards.back: Through segmentation and isolation/sandboxing/containerisation — risky or suspicious processes run in an isolated environment, reducing the attack surface.

cards.front: Give security issues with BYOD.
cards.back: Organisational data on a personal device, password policy enforcement, privacy, securing data on/off the device, patching/compatibility, and wiping company data when no longer needed.

cards.front: Security issues of remote working?
cards.back: Devices seen/used by family or visitors, insecure home Wi-Fi, reliance on third-party tools (e.g. video calls) — needs a VPN/encrypted link and secure home network.

cards.front: Switch vs router vs gateway?
cards.back: Switch connects devices within a LAN. Router joins different networks and directs packets between them. Gateway translates between different protocols/networks.

cards.front: Security issues of external media?
cards.back: Loss/theft, interception/copying, data loss/corruption, limited lifespan/failure, and acting as a malware vector — mitigated by encryption and secure disposal.

cards.front: What is TCP/IP?
cards.back: The core protocol suite for transmitting data over networks. Uses a four-layer model, sends data as packets with headers, includes error correction, and uses TLS for secure connections.

cards.front: What are the parts of a packet?
cards.back: Header (source/destination addresses and control info), payload/body (the actual data), and trailer/footer (error-checking). Types include TCP, IP and UDP.

cards.front: TCP vs UDP?
cards.back: TCP is reliable — it checks packets arrive and re-sends lost ones (good for files/web). UDP is faster but doesn't guarantee delivery (good for streaming/VoIP).

cards.front: What is NAT?
cards.back: Network Address Translation maps private internal IP addresses to a public IP address, letting many devices share one public IP and hiding the internal network.

cards.front: Name the RFC 1918 private IP ranges.
Security benefits of network segmentation?
cards.back: Limits access to devices/data/apps, restricts lateral movement of an attacker/malware, creates a smaller attack surface, and makes damage control simpler.

cards.front: Which device gives secure internet access on a network diagram?
cards.back: A firewall — placed between the router/internet connection and the internal network to filter traffic. (Sample paper Q1: add a firewall connected to the router.)

cards.front: What does DNS do?
cards.back: The Domain Name System resolves human-readable domain names (e.g. example.com) into IP addresses so devices can connect. Can be attacked via DNS spoofing/poisoning.

cards.front: What is DHCP and why is it insecure?
cards.back: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol automatically assigns IP addresses/settings to devices. It's insecure because it has NO built-in security, leaving it open to spoofing/rogue-server attacks.

cards.front: Name pieces of DHCP configuration information.
cards.back: Range of available IP addresses, fixed/reserved IP addresses, lease length/information, default gateway address, and server address.

cards.front: How does a VPN work?
cards.back: It creates an encrypted 'tunnel' over the public internet between the user and the network, so that even if data is intercepted it cannot be read. Used for secure remote access.

cards.front: Why are SMTP/POP email protocols a security weakness?
cards.back: They lack built-in encryption, so email content can be intercepted and read in transit unless additional security (e.g. TLS) is added.

cards.front: Physical vs logical topology?
cards.back: Physical topology is the actual layout of devices/cables (star, mesh, etc.). Logical topology is how data actually flows through the network (logical bus or ring).

cards.front: What is a packet sniffer used for?
cards.back: A network analyser/packet sniffer captures and inspects network traffic — used for monitoring/troubleshooting, but also by attackers to eavesdrop on unencrypted data.

cards.front: What is the Plan-Do-Check-Act loop?
cards.back: A continuous improvement cycle (from ISO 27001) used in a cyber security policy — security is never 'finished' because threats keep changing, so you keep planning, doing, checking and acting.

cards.front: What should a password policy contain?
cards.back: Length/complexity, password sharing rules, uniqueness/reuse frequency, minimum/maximum age, expiry, lockout after failed attempts, and deny lists of common passwords.

cards.front: Features of effective staff security training?
cards.back: Funded/resourced by management, flexible so everyone can take part, varied resources/learning styles, progress tracking, incentives rather than punishment, and ongoing for new threats.

cards.front: What is a security audit?
cards.back: A check of whether the organisation complies with its security policies and external laws/regulations, identifying gaps/weaknesses and reporting required improvements.

cards.front: What should a backup policy include?
cards.back: What data is selected, backup method and type, frequency/scheduling, storage strategy, responsibility/accountability, backup TESTING, and legal/recovery procedures.

cards.front: Stages of a cyber security incident response?
cards.back: Triage/escalation (initial decisions) → main response (analysis, containment, mitigation, recovery) → reviewing, reporting and closing the incident.

cards.front: Who should be on an incident response contact list?
cards.back: Incident response lead, IT team lead, senior management, legal, public relations, human resources and insurance — plus backup contact numbers.

cards.front: What is triage in a disaster recovery policy?
cards.back: Listing possible events, rating their severity, and deciding the appropriate response — e.g. activate incident response, the business continuity plan, or the full disaster recovery plan.

cards.front: What does an external services policy cover?
cards.back: Use of external providers for cloud, hardware, software and support — including authorisation, accountability, compliance, service agreements (SLAs) and incident response.

cards.front: Key elements of a data protection policy?
cards.back: Appoint a Data Protection Officer, follow GDPR principles, protect rights/privacy, staff training, system security procedures, and apply the policy to external contractors.

cards.front: Why use a Faraday bag/cage when seizing a device?
cards.back: It blocks all wireless signals so the device cannot communicate or be remotely wiped, preserving the evidence on it.

cards.front: What is chain of custody?
cards.back: A documented record of everyone who has handled a piece of evidence and what they did with it — proves the evidence hasn't been tampered with, keeping it admissible.

cards.front: Why is live forensics challenging?
cards.back: Data in active memory (RAM) and temporary files are lost when the device is switched off; data changes while the system runs; and remote/corrupted data is hard to capture.

cards.front: What are contemporaneous notes?
cards.back: Notes made AT THE TIME of the investigation. They improve the reliability and admissibility of evidence because they record exactly what was observed and done.

cards.front: Physical image vs targeted image of a drive?
cards.back: A physical image copies the ENTIRE drive — including deleted, temporary and system files — capturing more potential evidence. A targeted image copies only selected files, so it could miss evidence.

cards.front: Why generate a hash/checksum of a forensic image?
cards.back: To prove the copy is identical to the original and hasn't been altered — if the hash still matches later, the evidence's integrity is verified.

cards.front: Why work from a copy/image, not the original device?
cards.back: Any change to the original data could make it inadmissible in court. Working on a copy preserves the original evidence untouched.

cards.front: What is 'alert fatigue'?
cards.back: When a system produces so many alerts (often false positives) that investigators stop paying proper attention — risking missing a real threat. Reduced by tuning detection and manual review.

cards.front: Name signs that a system has been compromised.
cards.back: Unusual inbound/outbound traffic (or from odd regions), unusual login attempts, unusual DNS requests, increased file reads/requests, unusual port usage, and suspicious file changes.

cards.front: What should a security report contain?
cards.back: A clear structure (title, contents, intro, headings, conclusions, citations), analysis of what went wrong (procedure/detection/prevention errors), and recommended improvements to policies and protection measures.

cards.front: What must you do before network forensic scanning?
cards.back: Agree a methodology with the relevant authorities, get permission, and ensure the testing protocol will not disrupt the live system.

cards.front: Steps to isolate a seized device from networks?
cards.back: Photograph the screen, then turn off the device / remove the battery / use airplane mode / disable wireless / place it in a Faraday bag — so it can't be remotely wiped.
